claims.text: High-entropy alloys commonly contain at least five elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic proportions and can form random solid solutions.
An equiatomic Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti alloy is a suitable example of the proposed initial HEA.
The initial Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti HEA is single-phase and has a random solid-solution structure.
Controlled processing can dissolve oxygen uniformly at interstitial sites without producing large oxide precipitates.
High-temperature processing under a controlled atmosphere can ensure uniform oxygen uptake and retention in interstitial sites while minimizing secondary phases.
Interstitial atoms in Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti-based HEAs can occupy multiple configurations, including ordered complexes and randomly distributed sites.
The complex composition of HEAs creates a multitude of local chemical environments for interstitial atoms.
Adding interstitial oxygen increases lattice distortion in the HEA.
Interstitial oxygen modifies the local chemical environments in the HEA.
Interstitial oxygen produces local lattice strain and changes the electronic environment.
Oxygen-induced lattice strain and electronic changes adjust magnetic exchange interactions in the alloy.
Adjusted magnetic exchange interactions can increase the magnetic entropy change under an applied magnetic field.
Oxygen-doped Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti HEA will exhibit a larger magnetic entropy change than an oxygen-free counterpart.
Oxygen doping will improve the cooling capacity of the HEA.
There is a narrow oxygen-concentration window in which lattice distortion is beneficial.
Excessive oxygen can cause oxide precipitation and degrade magnetic and mechanical properties.
Direct evidence that interstitial oxygen improves magnetocaloric properties in HEAs is limited.
The proposed magnetocaloric mechanism is extrapolated from interstitial relaxation behavior in HEAs rather than demonstrated magnetic measurements.
